newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso says fiscal situation tranquil.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso says fiscal situation tranquil.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said on Monday that he viewed Brazil's fiscal situation and a surge in internal debt with tranquillity.
"The government has a lot of control (over the fiscal situation)," he said during a current affairs talk show on state-run TV Nacional. "Everything's tranquil."

Cardoso said Brasilia would have taken action if there were concern about internal debt, which has more than doubled since he took office in January 1995 to reach 217.644 billion reais in July, or 30.3 percent of gross domestic product.

Cardoso, interviewed by journalists on the Roda Viva television show, said the two most difficult periods he has faced were the aftermath of the Mexican peso crisis and a crisis facing the financial system halfway through last year.
But he said the government's PROER plan to encourage mergers and acquisitions in the banking sector had alleviated the worst problems at a relatively small cost.
Cardoso said the PROER plan, which provides banks with low cost credit lines for takeovers or mergers, had cost Brazil some 10 billion reais so far, or about 1.5 percent of GDP.
Cardoso said that compared extremely favourably with other Latin American countries where salvaging the financial system has cost up to 15 percent of GDP, as in Venezuela.
Last week, the government announced a series of fiscal measures intended to reduce next year's operational deficit to 2.5 percent of GDP from an expected 3.5 percent of GDP this year.

Officials say the cost-cutting and revenue-raising package is intended to show Brazil can tackle the fiscal problems without relying entirely on an at times recalcitrant Congress to approve key fiscal reforms.
The Brazilian president defended Congress, saying a lot had been accomplished, but he added, "Clearly it's not enough".
Cardoso said the main problem facing the Brazilian economy was the finances of the states and municipalities.
The government last month began refinancing the debts of the states, 12 of which are thought to be technically bankrupt, in return for fiscal adjustments and asset sales.
"We will help any state willing to help itself," Cardoso said.
